learnings.title: The LLD round — what 'design a component' actually means
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Increasingly the *other* frontend design round: no architecture diagram, no [CDN](/system-design/115), no rendering strategy. One component, forty-five minutes, and a much higher bar for detail.

## How it differs from the HLD round

| | HLD | LLD |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prompt | "Design a news feed" | "Design a data table component" |
| Deliverable | Boxes, boundaries, data flow | A **props API** and a state machine |
| Depth | Broad, three levels down on two topics | Narrow, five levels down on all of it |
| Grades | Architecture judgement | API taste, a11y, edge cases |
| You are | The architect | The library author |

The mental shift that matters: **you are designing a component other teams will use and you will not be there to explain it.** Every ambiguity in the API is a support question forever.

## The five stages

A RADIO equivalent for components:

### 1. Use cases (4–6 min)

Not "what does a table do" — *who calls this, and what do they need?*

> "Before I design the API I want to know the range. Is this for one admin screen, or is it a design-system component that forty teams will use? Those are different components — a shared one needs escape hatches and a stability guarantee that a one-screen table doesn't."

List the concrete callers: a read-only report, an editable grid, a selectable list feeding a bulk action. The API must serve all of them or you must say which you are cutting.

### 2. The API (10–12 min)

The centre of the round. Props, callbacks, composition shape, and what is [controlled vs uncontrolled](/react-guide/22). Write it out — actual TypeScript, not prose.

### 3. State and behaviour (8–10 min)

What state exists, where it lives, and what transitions are legal. For anything with real interaction, **draw the state machine.** "Open, closed, opening, closing" is a real distinction if there is an exit animation.

### 4. Accessibility (6–8 min)

Not a closing remark. Which ARIA pattern, what the keyboard contract is, where focus goes, what gets announced. In an LLD round this is often 25% of the score, because it is what separates a component from a `<div>` with a click handler.

### 5. Edge cases and performance (8–10 min)

Empty, loading, error, one item, ten thousand items, very long text, RTL, controlled/uncontrolled switching, unmount mid-async.

## What they are actually grading

| Signal | Weak | Strong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **API taste** | Fifteen boolean props | Composition plus variants, one way to do each thing |
| **Controlled/uncontrolled** | Never mentioned | Supports both, and knows why the pattern exists |
| **A11y** | "I'd add ARIA labels" | Names the pattern, the keyboard map, and the focus contract |
| **Edge cases** | Happy path only | Raises empty, error and unmount-mid-async unprompted |
| **Composition** | One component, every option | Compound parts with a documented escape hatch |

## The habits that score

**Write real types.** An interviewer can evaluate a type signature instantly; they cannot evaluate a description of one.

```typescript
type DataTableProps<Row> = {
  rows: Row[];
  columns: Column<Row>[];
  getRowId: (row: Row) => string;      // never trust array index
  sort?: SortState;                     // present = controlled
  defaultSort?: SortState;              // absent sort = uncontrolled
  onSortChange?: (next: SortState) => void;
  state?: 'loading' | 'ready' | 'empty' | 'error';
};
```

**Name the prior art.** "This is the [combobox](/system-design/302) pattern — I'd take the behaviour from Radix rather than hand-roll the ARIA" is not a dodge; it is what a senior engineer would actually do, and it tells the interviewer you know the pattern is hard.

**Say the escape hatch out loud.** "I'd add `asChild` so a team can render the trigger as their own button without forking the component." Components without escape hatches get forked, and forks are worse than flexibility.

## Common mistakes

- **Jumping to implementation.** They asked for a design; rendering logic is the least interesting part.
- **A boolean per variation.** `isPrimary` + `isLarge` + `isDisabled` + `isLoading` is four booleans and sixteen states, most of which are nonsense.
- **Accessibility at minute 43.** Too late to be a design decision.
- **Ignoring controlled vs uncontrolled.** The first thing a real consumer hits.
- **No empty or error state.** They are part of the component, not the caller's problem.
- **Designing for one caller** when you were told it is shared.

## Key takeaways

- Use cases, API, state, accessibility, edge cases — and the API is the centre.
- You are the library author; ambiguity in the API is a permanent support cost.
- Write real type signatures; they are evaluable in a way prose is not.
- Accessibility is roughly a quarter of the score, not a closing remark.
- Naming prior art for hard ARIA patterns is the senior answer, not a dodge.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How would a team customise the row rendering?"** — A render prop or a compound `Table.Row`. Then say which you prefer and why.
- **"What if they need something you didn't anticipate?"** — That is the escape-hatch question. Have an answer: a lower-level primitive, `asChild`, or a documented extension point.
- **"How do you version this?"** — Semver, dev-time deprecation warnings, a codemod for breaking changes. See the [design system](/system-design/108) entry.

learnings.title: Component API design — props, composition and control
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
The half of the [LLD round](/system-design/300) that decides your score. A component's API is a contract you cannot easily change once forty call sites depend on it, and interviewers know it.

## The four API shapes

### 1. Configuration props

```javascript
<Select options={options} value={v} onChange={setV} placeholder="Pick one" />;
```

Simple, discoverable, and **rigid**. The first consumer who needs a custom option row has no path but to fork. Right for genuinely simple components.

### 2. Render props / children as a function

```javascript
<Select options={options} renderOption={(o) => <Flag country={o.code} />} />;
```

Flexible and explicit about what the component controls. Gets ugly fast with more than two or three.

### 3. Compound components

```javascript
<Select.Root value={v} onValueChange={setV}>
  <Select.Trigger>
    <Select.Value />
  </Select.Trigger>
  <Select.Content>
    {options.map((o) => (
      <Select.Item key={o.id} value={o.id}>
        {o.label}
      </Select.Item>
    ))}
  </Select.Content>
</Select.Root>;
```

**Usually the right answer for anything non-trivial.** Structure is explicit, each part is individually styleable, and shared state travels through context rather than prop-drilling. The cost is more to type and a structure the consumer can get wrong.

### 4. Headless hook

```javascript
const { getTriggerProps, getMenuProps, getItemProps, isOpen } = useSelect({
  items,
});
```

Maximum flexibility, zero opinion about markup. Right for a component whose *behaviour* is hard and whose *appearance* varies wildly.

> "I'd go compound. Configuration props are one custom row away from a fork, and a headless hook pushes all the ARIA back onto every consumer — which is the thing I most want to solve once."

## Controlled and uncontrolled — do not skip this

The pattern everyone uses and few can articulate:

```javascript
function useControllableState({ value, defaultValue, onChange }) {
  const [uncontrolled, setUncontrolled] = useState(defaultValue);
  // Presence of `value` — not its truthiness — decides the mode.
  const isControlled = value !== undefined;
  const state = isControlled ? value : uncontrolled;

  const setState = useCallback(
    (next) => {
      if (!isControlled) setUncontrolled(next);
      onChange?.(next); // fires in BOTH modes
    },
    [isControlled, onChange],
  );

  return [state, setState];
}
```

Three rules that are easy to get wrong:

1. **Mode is decided by `value !== undefined`**, never by truthiness. `value={0}` and `value=""` are legitimate controlled values.
2. **`onChange` fires in both modes.** An uncontrolled component that goes silent is useless for analytics and for side effects.
3. **Warn in development if a component switches modes** mid-life. React does this for inputs for good reason — it is always a bug.

## Variants over booleans

```typescript
// Four booleans = sixteen combinations, most of them meaningless.
<Button isPrimary isLarge isDanger isGhost />

// A closed set of legal states, expressible in the type system.
<Button variant="danger" size="lg" />
```

Booleans multiply; variants enumerate. `variant="primary" variant="ghost"` cannot both be true, and the type system enforces it.

## The escape hatch

Components without one get forked, and a fork is worse than the flexibility you refused:

```javascript
// asChild renders the child element instead of the default, merging
// props and behaviour into it.
<Tooltip.Trigger asChild>
  <MyCustomButton />
</Tooltip.Trigger>;
```

Plus: forward `className` and `...rest` to the root, forward refs, and export the lower-level primitives so a consumer who needs to go deeper can, without copy-pasting your source.

## Callback naming and payloads

```typescript
// `onChange` fires on every keystroke; `onValueCommit` on blur or Enter.
// Two events because consumers genuinely need both.
onChange?: (value: string) => void;
onValueCommit?: (value: string) => void;

// Pass the VALUE, not the event. The consumer almost never wants
// the event, and passing it leaks your implementation.
onSelect?: (item: Item) => void;        // not (e: MouseEvent)
```

Name events for **what happened**, not what the user did: `onValueChange` rather than `onClick`, because the same change can arrive from the keyboard.

## State: what the component owns

The rule: **own presentation, expose meaning.**

| Component owns | Consumer owns |
| --- | --- |
| Whether the menu is open (with `open`/`onOpenChange` to override) | Which item is selected |
| Highlighted index during keyboard navigation | The list of items |
| Internal animation state | Loading and error state |
| [Focus management](/system-design/406) | What selection means |

Anything the consumer might need to control must be *controllable* — but should still have a working uncontrolled default.

## Common mistakes

- **A boolean per variation.** Combinatorial explosion of meaningless states.
- **Mode by truthiness** rather than `!== undefined`.
- **`onChange` only in controlled mode.**
- **Passing the DOM event** instead of the value.
- **No escape hatch.** Guarantees forks.
- **Not forwarding refs or `className`.** Blocks positioning, testing and styling.
- **Owning state the consumer needs**, with no way to control it.

## Key takeaways

- [Compound components](/react-guide/21) are usually right for anything with real structure; headless when behaviour is hard and appearance varies.
- Support controlled and uncontrolled; mode is `value !== undefined` and `onChange` fires in both.
- Variants, not booleans — enumerate legal states instead of multiplying them.
- Ship a documented escape hatch, forward refs and `className`.
- Own presentation; expose meaning.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How do you stop the API sprawling over two years?"** — A deliberate escape hatch absorbs one-off needs without new props, and every new prop must serve more than one caller.
- **"Compound components feel verbose."** — They are. The trade is explicit structure and per-part styling; for a simple component it is not worth it, and I'd use configuration props there.
- **"How would you type the compound parts?"** — Shared state through a typed context, with a dev-time error if a part is rendered outside its root.

learnings.title: Design an autocomplete component
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
The LLD twin of the autocomplete case study. There, the question was the network race. Here it is the **API** and the **combobox pattern** — and the combobox is one of the two or three hardest ARIA patterns there is. ## The API ```typescript type ComboboxProps = { items: Item[]; // The component never fetches. The caller owns the async; // that is what lets the same component do local filtering, // remote search, or a static list. onInputValueChange?: (value: string) => void; isLoading?: boolean; value?: Item | null; // controlled defaultValue?: Item | null; onChange?: (item: Item | null) => void; itemToString: (item: Item) => string; // for the input and the a11y name getItemId: (item: Item) => string; // The three states that are always forgotten. emptyMessage?: ReactNode; errorMessage?: ReactNode; loadingMessage?: ReactNode; allowCustomValue?: boolean; // free text vs strict selection openOnFocus?: boolean; }; ``` **The component does not fetch.** It reports what was typed and renders what it is given. That keeps the race-condition handling — [debounce](/coding/13), abort, sequence guard — in the caller's data layer where it belongs, and makes the component testable with a plain array. `allowCustomValue` is a genuine fork worth raising: a country picker must reject anything not in the list; a tag input must accept new values. Same pattern, opposite rule. ## The state machine Worth drawing, because the transitions are where the bugs live: ```mermaid stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Closed Closed --> Open: focus / type / ArrowDown Open --> Open: type (filter, reset highlight) Open --> Open: ArrowUp/Down (move highlight) Open --> Closed: Escape (keep text) Open --> Selected: Enter / click Selected --> Closed: commit + fill input Open --> Closed: blur (revert if strict) ``` ```typescript { inputValue: 'reac', isOpen: true, highlightedIndex: 2, // -1 = nothing highlighted selectedItem: null, } ``` **`highlightedIndex` is not focus.** DOM focus stays in the input for the entire interaction — that is the single most important fact about this pattern. ## Accessibility — the combobox pattern ```html
  • react
8 results available
``` The keyboard contract: | Key | Behaviour | | --- | --- | | `ArrowDown` | Open if closed; otherwise move the highlight down (wrap or stop — pick one) | | `ArrowUp` | Move up; from the first item, back to the input with no highlight | | `Enter` | Select the highlighted item; if nothing is highlighted, submit or do nothing | | `Escape` | Close and keep the typed text. A second `Escape` clears it | | `Tab` | Close and commit or revert per `allowCustomValue` — never trap `Tab` | | `Home` / `End` | First / last item | The non-obvious rules: - **Focus never leaves the input.** Moving real focus into the list breaks typing and breaks screen readers. - **Announce the result count** in a polite live region. Without it, a [screen reader](/system-design/406) user has no idea a list appeared. - **Reset the highlight when the query changes.** Keeping index 2 across a new result set selects an unrelated item on Enter — a real, damaging bug. - **Scroll the highlighted option into view**, using `scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest' })` so it does not jump the page. ## Mouse and touch details - **Hover sets the highlight**, so mouse and keyboard share one concept of "current". - **Use `onMouseDown` with `preventDefault` on options**, not `onClick`. A click fires after blur, and by then the list has closed — this is the classic "clicking a suggestion does nothing" bug. - Touch targets ≥ 44 px, and the list must not be covered by the on-screen keyboard. ## Rendering and performance - **Virtualize above ~100 options.** With [virtualization](/react-guide/16), `aria-activedescendant` must point at a rendered element, so keep the highlighted item in the rendered window. - **Portal the list** so it escapes `overflow: hidden` ancestors; then you need collision detection to flip it above the input near the bottom of the viewport. This is exactly the part worth taking from Floating UI rather than hand-rolling. - Memoise the option rows; a list re-rendering on every keystroke is a real cost on a mid-range phone. ## Multi-select A distinct enough variation to mention: - Selected items render as removable chips **before** the input - `Backspace` on an empty input removes the last chip — expected, and always missed - `aria-multiselectable="true"` on the listbox, `aria-selected` per option - The list stays open after a selection ## Edge cases to raise unprompted Zero results (a message, never an empty box) · a slow request (delay the spinner ~300 ms) · a failed request (keep the input usable) · IME composition (do not filter mid-composition) · paste (search immediately, skip the debounce) · a very long option label (truncate visually, keep the full accessible name) · the selected item no longer in the list. ## Common mistakes - **Fetching inside the component.** Locks it to one data source and buries the race handling. - **Moving focus into the list.** Breaks typing and screen readers. - **`onClick` on options.** Blur closes the list first. - **Not resetting the highlight on query change.** Enter selects the wrong item. - **No live region.** Silence for screen reader users. - **Trapping `Tab`.** Users must be able to leave. - **No empty state.** ## Key takeaways - The component renders and reports; the caller owns the async and the race. - Focus stays in the input; `aria-activedescendant` carries the highlight. - Reset the highlight whenever the item list changes. - `onMouseDown` + `preventDefault`, not `onClick`. - Announce counts politely and always design the empty state. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Async items?"** — The component takes `items` and `isLoading`; debounce, abort and sequence-guard live in the caller's hook. Show the previous results while loading rather than blanking. - **"Grouped results?"** — `role="group"` with `aria-labelledby` inside the listbox; keyboard navigation stays one flat sequence across groups, and headers are not selectable. - **"Why not a native `

learnings.title: Design a modal / dialog system
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Small surface, unusually deep. Almost the entire question is **[focus management](/system-design/406)**, and it is the component where a [design system](/system-design/108) most obviously earns its cost — because forty teams will each get this wrong in a slightly different way. ## Use cases Alert (message + acknowledge) · confirm (destructive action) · form dialog · full-screen on mobile · nested (a confirm on top of a form) · non-modal popover. > "Is it a *modal* dialog — the rest of the page is inert — or a non-modal panel? That decides whether I need a focus trap at all, and it's the difference between two very different components." ## The API ```typescript type DialogProps = { open?: boolean; // controlled defaultOpen?: boolean; // uncontrolled onOpenChange?: (open: boolean) => void; // Escape hatches for the cases where the defaults are wrong. closeOnEscape?: boolean; // default true closeOnOutsideClick?: boolean; // default true; false for forms initialFocus?: RefObject; // default: first focusable returnFocus?: RefObject; // default: whatever opened it size?: 'sm' | 'md' | 'lg' | 'full'; }; // Compound, so the parts are individually styleable and the title // can be wired to aria-labelledby automatically. Delete project? This cannot be undone. ``` `Dialog.Title` is not decorative — the component wires it to `aria-labelledby` automatically. That is how a compound API makes the accessible thing the default thing. ## The focus contract Six rules. Missing any one of them produces a dialog that is unusable by keyboard: 1. **On open, move focus into the dialog** — the first focusable element, or the dialog itself if there is none. Not doing this leaves focus behind the overlay. 2. **Trap focus.** `Tab` from the last element wraps to the first; `Shift+Tab` from the first wraps to the last. 3. **On close, restore focus to what opened it.** Without this, focus falls to `` and a keyboard user is thrown to the top of the page. 4. **`Escape` closes.** Always, unless there is unsaved work — and then ask rather than silently ignoring the key. 5. **Make the background inert**, so a screen reader cannot browse past the dialog into content that is visually hidden behind it. 6. **Lock body scroll** without shifting the layout. ### The modern way to do it ```javascript // gives you the focus trap, the inert background, Escape, // and the top layer — natively. dialogRef.current.showModal(); ``` `` handles most of this correctly, and the top layer means no `z-index` war. The gaps you still own: initial focus placement (it focuses the first focusable, which may be a close button), returning focus on close, and scroll locking. If you cannot use it, `inert` on the background is the modern replacement for `aria-hidden` juggling: ```javascript // One attribute makes a whole subtree unfocusable and invisible to AT. document.getElementById("root").inert = open; ``` ### Scroll locking without the jump ```javascript // Naive `overflow: hidden` removes the scrollbar and the page jumps // by its width. Compensate. const gap = window.innerWidth - document.documentElement.clientWidth; document.body.style.overflow = "hidden"; document.body.style.paddingRight = `${gap}px`; ``` On iOS Safari `overflow: hidden` on `body` does not reliably stop scrolling; `position: fixed` with a saved scroll offset is the usual workaround, and it must restore the position on close. ## Stacking — the part people miss A confirm dialog on top of a form dialog: ```javascript // A stack, not a boolean. Escape closes only the TOP dialog; // only the top dialog traps focus. const stack = useRef([]); function open(id) { stack.current.push(id); } function close(id) { stack.current = stack.current.filter((x) => x !== id); } const isTop = stack.current.at(-1) === id; ``` With a naive per-dialog implementation, `Escape` closes both, or the wrong one, or focus is trapped in the dialog underneath. A **shared dialog manager** is what makes nesting correct — and it is a good example of why this belongs in a design system rather than in each feature. ## Accessibility details ```html
``` - `role="alertdialog"` for destructive confirms — it is announced more assertively - `aria-modal="true"` **only** alongside a real focus trap and inert background; lying about it is worse than omitting it - The title must exist. A dialog announced as "dialog" tells the user nothing. - A visible, focusable close control — not an icon with no accessible name - Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` on the enter/exit transitions ## Mobile Full-screen below a breakpoint rather than a small centred card. Watch the on-screen keyboard: `100vh` is wrong when the keyboard is up; use `100dvh`. Ensure the submit button is not hidden behind the keyboard. ## Common mistakes - **No focus restore on close.** Keyboard users are thrown to the top of the page. - **Focus trap only on `Tab`.** Screen readers browse by heading, not by Tab — you need `inert`. - **`aria-modal` without a real trap.** A lie to assistive technology. - **No title, or a title not wired to `aria-labelledby`.** - **Per-dialog state instead of a stack.** Nesting breaks. - **Scroll lock that shifts the layout.** - **Outside-click-to-close on a form dialog.** Deletes work with one stray click. ## Key takeaways - The whole component is a focus contract: move in, trap, restore, Escape, inert, scroll lock. - Prefer native `` — it gives you the trap, inert and the top layer. - Use `inert` on the background; a Tab trap alone does not stop a screen reader browsing past. - Nesting requires a shared stack; only the top dialog traps and responds to Escape. - Never outside-click-to-close a dialog containing unsaved work. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Why not just `aria-hidden` the background?"** — It hides from screen readers but leaves elements focusable. `inert` does both, in one attribute. - **"An async confirm that can fail?"** — A pending state that disables the confirm, and an error rendered inside the dialog. Never close the dialog before the action has succeeded. - **"How do you test it?"** — Keyboard-only walkthrough: open, Tab to wrap, Escape, and assert focus is back on the trigger. That is four assertions and it catches most of the real bugs.

learnings.title: Design a form library
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
A question about **re-render economics** as much as API design: the naive design re-renders forty fields on every keystroke, and on a mid-range phone that is felt. ## The API ```typescript const form = useForm({ defaultValues: { email: '', password: '' }, resolver: zodResolver(schema), // validation is pluggable, not built in mode: 'onTouched', // when to validate — see below });
``` **Validation is a plugged-in resolver, not a built-in DSL.** Zod, Yup and Valibot already exist, callers often already have a schema, and the same schema can validate on the server. Inventing a validation language is a decade of edge cases nobody asked for. ## Uncontrolled by default — the performance decision ```javascript // Controlled: every keystroke is a state update in the form's owner, // so every field re-renders. 40 fields × every keystroke. const [values, setValues] = useState({}); // Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value; the library holds a ref. // A keystroke re-renders NOTHING until validation has something to say. const { ref, ...rest } = register("email"); ; ``` This is the reason React Hook Form beats Formik on any large form, and being able to explain it is the point of the question. The trade you must name: uncontrolled inputs are harder to drive programmatically, so the library needs `setValue`, `reset` and `watch` — and `watch` re-introduces subscriptions, which is exactly why it must be **granular**. ### Granular subscriptions ```javascript // Subscribe to ONE field. Only components reading `email` re-render. const email = useWatch({ control, name: "email" }); // Subscribe to one field's error, not the whole error object. const { error } = useFormState({ control, name: "email" }); ``` A single `formState` object that every field reads defeats the entire design — any change to it re-renders everything. The store must be subscribable per field path. ## State model ```typescript { values: Map, // refs, not React state errors: Map, touched: Set, dirty: Set, isSubmitting: false, submitCount: 0, } ``` Paths are strings — `'address.line1'`, `'items.2.qty'` — so nested and array fields need no special casing in the store. Array operations (`append`, `remove`, `move`) are a separate concern: ```javascript const { fields, append, remove, move } = useFieldArray({ control, name: "items", }); // `fields` carries a stable generated `id` per row. Keying an array // field by index means removing row 2 visually clears row 3's input, // because React reuses the DOM node. ``` That index-keying bug is one of the most common in real forms and worth calling out. ## Validation timing The rule that makes a form feel fair rather than hostile: | Mode | Validates | Use | | --- | --- | --- | | `onSubmit` | Only on submit | Short forms | | `onTouched` | On blur after first touch, then on change | **The sensible default** | | `onChange` | Every keystroke | Almost always too aggressive | | `all` | Blur and change | Live password strength meters | The asymmetry that matters: **validate lazily, clear eagerly.** Do not show an error while someone is still typing their email — but once an error is showing, re-validate on every keystroke so it disappears the instant it is fixed. ### Async validation ```javascript // "Is this username taken?" — debounced, cancellable, and it must not // block submit indefinitely. const resolver = async (values) => { const sync = schema.safeParse(values); if (!sync.success) return { errors: format(sync.error) }; const taken = await checkUsername(values.username, { signal }); return taken ? { errors: { username: "Already taken" } } : { values }; }; ``` Race conditions apply here exactly as in autocomplete — [debounce](/coding/13), abort, and ignore a response for a value that is no longer current. ## Accessibility Non-negotiable, and the library should make it automatic rather than optional: ```html

We'll never share it

Enter a valid email address

``` - Every field has a real `

learnings.title: Design a date picker
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Deceptive. It looks like a grid of numbers and is really an [internationalisation](/system-design/409) and accessibility problem — and the correct first answer is often "use the native input". ## Start by questioning the premise > "Does this need to be a custom picker? On mobile, `` gives the OS picker, which people already know, is fully accessible, and is correctly localised for free. I'd use native unless we need a range, disabled dates, or a design the native control can't express." That answer scores well because it is what an experienced engineer would actually do. Custom pickers exist for range selection, availability constraints, and multi-month views — not for aesthetics. ## The API ```typescript type DatePickerProps = { value?: Date | null; // controlled defaultValue?: Date | null; onChange?: (date: Date | null) => void; min?: Date; max?: Date; isDateDisabled?: (date: Date) => boolean; // availability, blackouts locale?: string; // default: navigator.language weekStartsOn?: 0 | 1; // default: derived from locale timeZone?: string; mode?: 'single' | 'range' | 'multiple'; numberOfMonths?: number; // 2 for a range picker }; ``` `isDateDisabled` as a predicate rather than an array is what makes this usable for booking — "no Sundays, and these 40 specific dates" is a function, not a list. ## Internationalisation — most of the difficulty Use `Intl` for everything. Hand-rolling any of this is wrong: ```javascript // Weekday names, in the right language AND the right order. const fmt = new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { weekday: "short" }); // The week does not start on Sunday everywhere. It starts on Monday // in most of Europe, Saturday in much of the Middle East. const weekInfo = new Intl.Locale(locale).weekInfo; // { firstDay: 1, … } ``` | Concern | The rule | | --- | --- | | **Week start** | Locale-dependent — never hard-code Sunday | | **Non-Gregorian calendars** | Islamic, Hebrew, Japanese eras exist; `Intl` supports them | | **RTL** | The grid mirrors, but the **dates do not reverse** — only the layout direction changes | | **Date format** | `01/02/2026` is ambiguous. Use `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, and prefer a written month in confirmations | | **Time zones** | A "date" with no time is a wall-clock concept; converting through UTC can move it by a day | That last one is the classic bug: storing a date-only value as a UTC instant and rendering it in a different zone shows the previous day. **A date with no time should be stored as a plain `YYYY-MM-DD` string**, not as a `Date`. ## The keyboard grid The picker is `role="grid"` — a genuine grid, where arrow keys move by day: | Key | Moves | | --- | --- | | `ArrowLeft` / `ArrowRight` | ±1 day, crossing month boundaries | | `ArrowUp` / `ArrowDown` | ±1 week | | `Home` / `End` | Start / end of the week | | `PageUp` / `PageDown` | ±1 month | | `Shift+PageUp` / `PageDown` | ±1 year | | `Enter` / `Space` | Select | | `Escape` | Close, keeping the input's text | **Roving tabindex:** exactly one date cell is tabbable, so `Tab` enters and leaves the grid rather than walking 35 cells. ```html
Mo
``` **The accessible name must be the full date.** "12" is meaningless when read out of context, and this is the single most common date-picker accessibility failure. Announce month changes in a polite live region — a [screen reader](/system-design/406) user pressing `PageDown` otherwise has no idea the grid changed. ## Always allow typing A calendar grid is slower than typing for anyone who knows the date they want. The input must accept text, and parsing is locale-aware: ```javascript // Be generous in what you accept: 12/09/2026, 12-09-2026, 12 Sep 2026. // Then reformat to the canonical display form on blur so the user // can see how it was interpreted — which is how you avoid the // day/month ambiguity silently biting someone. ``` Show the interpreted date in unambiguous form ("12 September 2026") next to the input or in the confirmation. ## Range mode - Two months side by side on desktop, one on mobile - **Hovering previews the range** between the anchor and the hovered date — and the preview needs a keyboard equivalent, driven by the focused cell - Selecting a second date before the first swaps them rather than erroring - Announce the range, not just the endpoints: "12 to 19 September, 8 nights" ## Edge cases to raise unprompted DST transitions (a day can be 23 or 25 hours long) · leap years and 29 February · `min`/`max` crossing a month boundary, which must disable the navigation button too · a disabled date being the currently focused one · the picker opening near the viewport bottom (flip it) · a locale with a non-Gregorian calendar · very small viewports where a two-month range view does not fit. ## Common mistakes - **Building a custom picker when native would do.** - **Hard-coding Sunday as the week start.** - **`aria-label` of just the day number.** - **Storing a date-only value as a UTC `Date`.** Off-by-one-day across zones. - **No keyboard grid navigation.** - **No typed input.** Slow for everyone who knows the date. - **Hand-rolled month and weekday names.** ## Key takeaways - Ask whether native `` is enough first — often it is. - `Intl` for weekday names, week start, formatting and calendars; never hard-code. - Date-only values are `YYYY-MM-DD` strings, not instants. - `role="grid"` with a roving tabindex and full-date accessible names. - Always support typing, and echo back the interpreted date unambiguously. ## Interview follow-ups - **"A booking picker with unavailable dates?"** — `isDateDisabled` as a predicate, `aria-disabled` rather than removing the cell from the tab order (so it can still be discovered and explained), and a legend for why. - **"Date and time together?"** — Separate controls. A combined grid is harder to operate and much harder to make accessible; two inputs beat one clever widget. - **"Why not Moment.js?"** — Deprecated and large. `Intl` plus `Temporal`, or date-fns for tree-shakeable functions.

learnings.title: Design a carousel / image gallery
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Famously one of the most abused components on the web, and for that reason a good accessibility test. The strongest answers begin by questioning whether it should auto-play at all. ## Start with the premise > "Is it a hero carousel that rotates marketing slides, or a product image gallery the user drives? The first has terrible engagement data and real accessibility problems; the second is genuinely useful. If it's the first, I'd raise that — and if we still build it, it must not auto-play." Auto-rotating carousels are a WCAG problem (2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide) and a usability one. Saying so is not pedantry; it is the kind of product judgement senior interviews look for. ## The API ```typescript type CarouselProps = { children: ReactNode; // slides as children, not a data prop index?: number; // controlled defaultIndex?: number; onIndexChange?: (index: number) => void; loop?: boolean; // default false — see below autoPlay?: false | number; // interval ms; default false orientation?: 'horizontal' | 'vertical'; slidesPerView?: number | 'auto'; label: string; // required accessible name }; ``` **Slides as children, not a `slides` prop.** A slide can be an image, a card, a video — a data prop forces a `renderSlide` escape hatch immediately. **`autoPlay` defaults to `false`**, and `loop` defaults to `false` too: infinite loops make it impossible for a [screen reader](/system-design/406) user to know they have seen everything, and they break the "3 of 7" affordance. ## Scroll-snap over JavaScript The modern implementation is mostly CSS: ```css .viewport { display: flex; overflow-x: auto; scroll-snap-type: x mandatory; scrollbar-width: none; overscroll-behavior-x: contain; /* don't trigger browser back-swipe */ } .slide { flex: 0 0 100%; scroll-snap-align: start; } ``` ```javascript // Navigation is a scroll, not a transform. viewport.scrollTo({ left: index * slideWidth, behavior: "smooth" }); ``` Why this beats a JS-driven transform: - **Native momentum and touch physics** — hand-rolled drag never feels as good - **Keyboard scrolling works** for free - **Accessible by default**, because slides are in normal flow - Far less code, and it degrades gracefully Track the current index with an `IntersectionObserver` on the slides rather than a scroll handler — it is cheaper and correct during momentum scrolling. ## Accessibility Two valid patterns; pick and say which: **Carousel as a group** (recommended for galleries): ```html
…
Image 3 of 7
``` **Tabs pattern** (when the dots are the primary control): `role="tablist"` with `role="tabpanel"` slides — but then you owe the full tabs keyboard contract. The rules: - **Every slide announces its position** — "3 of 7". Without it, a screen reader user has no idea how many there are or where they are. - **Announce changes politely** in a live region. - **If it auto-plays, there must be a visible pause control**, and it must pause on hover, on focus, and when the tab is hidden. This is a WCAG requirement, not a nicety. - **Never `aria-hidden` the off-screen slides while they are still focusable** — a keyboard user tabs into content that screen readers are told does not exist. Use `inert` instead. - Respect `prefers-reduced-motion`: `behavior: 'auto'` instead of `'smooth'`, and no auto-play. ## Performance - **Lazy-load off-screen images** (`loading="lazy"`), but eagerly load slide 1 with `fetchpriority="high"` — it is often the LCP element - **Preload the adjacent slides** so navigation is instant - **Always set `width`/`height` or an `aspect-ratio` box** — a carousel without reserved space is a CLS generator - Use `srcset` — a gallery is the single largest payload on most product pages - For very many slides, virtualize: render current ± 2 and recycle ## Touch and pointer - With scroll-snap, touch is free and correct - If you must hand-roll drag: **Pointer Events**, `touch-action: pan-y` so vertical page scroll still works, and a velocity threshold so a fast flick advances even if the distance is short - `overscroll-behavior-x: contain` prevents an edge swipe triggering browser back navigation — an infuriating bug on iOS ## Edge cases to raise unprompted One slide (hide the controls entirely) · fewer slides than `slidesPerView` · slides of differing heights (fix the viewport height or the page jumps per slide) · a slide containing focusable content (focus must not land in an off-screen slide) · window resize changing slide width mid-scroll · RTL, where "next" is to the left · very slow images (a placeholder, never a blank slide). ## Common mistakes - **Auto-play with no pause control.** A WCAG failure. - **Infinite loop by default.** No way to know you have seen everything. - **No "3 of 7" position announcement.** - **`aria-hidden` on focusable off-screen slides.** - **Hand-rolled drag physics** when scroll-snap is better and free. - **No reserved aspect ratio.** Layout shift per slide. - **Controls with icon-only content and no accessible name.** - **Not disabling the browser back-swipe.** ## Key takeaways - Question auto-play first; if it stays, a pause control is mandatory. - CSS scroll-snap plus `IntersectionObserver` beats JS transforms on feel, code size and accessibility. - Every slide announces "n of m"; changes go to a polite live region. - Use `inert`, not `aria-hidden`, for off-screen slides. - Reserve aspect ratio, eager-load the first image, preload neighbours. ## Interview follow-ups - **"A thumbnail strip that syncs with the main image?"** — Two viewports sharing one controlled index; the thumbnails are a `tablist` and the main image its `tabpanel`. - **"Pinch to zoom on the full-size image?"** — A separate lightbox component; do not overload the carousel. The lightbox is a dialog and owes the full focus contract. - **"How do you test it?"** — Keyboard-only traversal, an assertion that off-screen slides are not focusable, and a check that auto-play stops on focus.

learnings.title: Design a chart component
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer: A component where the accessibility answer is genuinely interesting rather than a checklist — because a chart's information is encoded in pixels, and you have to put it somewhere else too. ## The API ```typescript type LineChartProps = { data: D[]; x: (d: D) => Date | number; y: (d: D) => number; series?: (d: D) => string; // grouping key for multi-series // Scales are an escape hatch, not a requirement. xScale?: ScaleConfig; yScale?: ScaleConfig; // Required. A chart with no description is inaccessible by // construction, so make it impossible to omit. title: string; summary: string; // the trend in words onPointClick?: (d: D) => void; height?: number; // width comes from the container }; ``` **Accessors, not a fixed data shape.** `x` and `y` as functions mean the caller never has to reshape their data to fit your component — which is the difference between a chart used everywhere and one wrapped in a mapping function at every call site. **`title` and `summary` are required props.** Making the accessible description non-optional is the single most effective thing the API can do. ## Composition ```javascript // Compound, because every chart needs a different combination of parts. d.date} y={(d) => d.value} height={320}> fmt.format(d)} /> ; ``` The parent owns scales, dimensions and the data; the children read them from context. A monolithic `` with thirty props cannot express "a line, an area, and one annotation" without thirty more. ## Rendering — pick by point count | Points | Renderer | | --- | --- | | < 1,000 | **SVG** — accessible, inspectable, CSS-styleable, easy hit-testing | | 1,000–100,000 | **Canvas** — SVG node count becomes the bottleneck | | > 100,000 | **Downsample first**, then canvas | **[Downsampling](/system-design/315) is usually the real answer.** A 1,200-pixel-wide chart has 1,200 columns; sending 100,000 points renders 98,800 of them on top of each other. Use **LTTB** (Largest-Triangle-Three-Buckets), which preserves the visual shape *including spikes*. Naive every-nth sampling can delete the spike that was the entire reason for looking at the chart. ## Responsiveness ```javascript // ResizeObserver, not a window resize listener — the container can // change size without the window doing so (a sidebar collapsing). const [width, setWidth] = useState(0); useLayoutEffect(() => { const ro = new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => setWidth(entry.contentRect.width)); ro.observe(containerRef.current); return () => ro.disconnect(); }, []); ``` Take width from the container and height from a prop. Axis labels need a responsive strategy too: rotate, drop every other, or abbreviate — but decide, because overlapping labels are the most common visual bug in charts. ## Accessibility — the interesting part A chart is a picture of data. Assistive technology needs the data. **1. A real text alternative that states the trend, not the pixels:** ```html ``` "A line chart showing data over time" is useless. The summary must contain the information the chart conveys. **2. A table view toggle.** The single most effective accessibility feature a chart can have — and sighted users reach for it constantly to read exact values. Same data, `` form, one control away. **3. Keyboard navigation of data points**, for interactive charts: arrow keys move between points, each announcing its value. **4. Never colour alone.** Series need dash patterns, markers, or direct labels. Around 8% of men have some colour vision deficiency, and red/green is the most common chart palette there is. **5. Contrast.** Series colours must meet contrast against the background *and* be distinguishable from each other and from gridlines. ## Tooltips - Follow the cursor but **clamp to the container**, so the tooltip near the right edge does not fall off screen - **Snap to the nearest data point**, do not interpolate — showing a value that does not exist in the data is worse than showing none - On touch, tap to pin; there is no hover - Never put information *only* in a tooltip; hover-only information is inaccessible by definition ## Edge cases to raise unprompted Empty data (an empty state, not empty axes) · a single point (no line to draw) · all values identical (the y-scale has zero range — pad it or the line sits on an axis) · negative values (the zero line matters) · missing points in a series (gap or interpolate — decide and be consistent) · very large numbers (abbreviate axis labels: 1.2M) · dates crossing a DST boundary · RTL, where the axis direction flips. ## Common mistakes - **A fixed data shape** instead of accessors. Every call site wraps it. - **Rendering 100,000 points into 1,200 pixels.** - **Every-nth downsampling.** Deletes the spikes. - **`window.resize` instead of `ResizeObserver`.** - **Colour-only series encoding.** - **A generic alt text** that conveys nothing. - **No table view.** - **Information available only on hover.** ## Key takeaways - Accessors, not a data shape; compound parts, not thirty props. - SVG below a thousand points, canvas above, and downsample with LTTB before either. - `ResizeObserver` on the container, with a deliberate axis-label strategy. - Make `title` and `summary` required so an inaccessible chart cannot be built. - Ship a table view; it is the best accessibility feature and everyone uses it. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Live updating?"** — Coalesce into `requestAnimationFrame`, append rather than re-render the whole series, and hold the axis domain stable so the chart does not rescale on every tick. - **"Zoom and pan?"** — Transform the scales, not the DOM, and refetch at higher resolution for the zoomed range. Provide keyboard zoom, or it is mouse-only. - **"Why not just use a chart library?"** — Usually you should. The question is whether you understand the trade-offs well enough to choose and configure one.

Design a multiplayer game communication system
learnings.source: user request: Acceldata LLD round prep, 16 Sep 2026
learnings.answer:
One of the two questions that actually gets asked by name. It looks like "build a chat box" and it is not — the grading happens in what you do when the network misbehaves, which in a game is constantly.

## Clarify before you design

The prompt is deliberately underspecified. Three questions change the whole answer, and asking them *is* part of the score:

| Question | Why it changes the design |
| --- | --- |
| **Chat, or game state sync?** | Chat tolerates 200ms and must never lose a message. Position updates tolerate loss and must never be late. Opposite designs — say which you are building. |
| **What channels exist?** | Global, team, party, whisper, proximity. Proximity means membership changes as players move, which is a subscription problem, not a UI one. |
| **Room size?** | 8 players is one broadcast. 10,000 in a global channel is a fan-out problem and probably needs rate limits and sampling. |

> "I'll assume text chat with global, team and whisper channels, rooms up to 64 players, and that position sync is a separate system — because it wants unreliable delivery and chat wants the opposite. Say if you'd rather I designed that instead."

That sentence buys you the rest of the round.

## Transport

WebSocket. Say why, briefly, and say what you rejected:

- **[SSE](/system-design/105)** is server→client only. Players send, so every message would become a separate `POST` — a full HTTP round trip to deliver forty bytes.
- **Long polling** works everywhere and costs a handshake per message. It is the fallback, not the design.
- **[Webhooks](/system-design/117)** are server-to-server; a game client has no address to receive one at.
- **WebTransport** is the interesting answer if the same connection also carries position updates — unreliable datagrams for positions, a reliable stream for chat, no [head-of-line blocking](/browser/161) between them. Raise it as a "where I'd go next", not as the primary, because of UDP blocking.

## The shape of it

![A multiplayer chat — one id, four states, one cursor](/diagrams/sysdesign/game-chat.svg)

## The message model

```typescript
type Message = {
  // Made by the CLIENT, before anything is sent. This is the idempotency key.
  id: string;
  channelId: string;
  senderId: string;

  // Made by the SERVER. Monotonic per channel — the ordering authority.
  seq?: number;
  serverTs?: number;

  body: string;
  state: "pending" | "sent" | "acked" | "failed";
};
```

Two facts carry most of the design:

**The client generates the id.** Not the server. That is what makes a retry safe: if the ack was lost but the message landed, the retry arrives with an id the server has already seen and is acknowledged rather than posted twice. Without it you cannot retry at all without risking duplicates, which means you cannot be reliable over an unreliable network.

**The server generates the order.** Never sort by `sentAt` from the client — clocks are wrong, and in a game some of them are wrong on purpose. `seq` is a per-channel counter; it is both the sort key and the gap detector.

## Optimistic send

```javascript
function send(channelId, body) {
  const msg = {
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),
    channelId,
    senderId: me.id,
    body,
    state: "pending",
  };

  store.append(msg); // on screen immediately — this is the whole point
  outbox.add(msg); // survives a disconnect
  flush();
}

function onAck({ id, seq, serverTs }) {
  // Reconcile by the id we invented, not by position or content.
  store.patch(id, { state: "acked", seq, serverTs });
  outbox.remove(id);
  reorderIfNeeded(id); // the server's seq may not match local append order
}
```

The detail worth saying out loud: **reconciling by id, not by index.** If you match the ack to "the last pending message" you break the moment two sends are in flight, which in a game is normal.

## Ordering, and the trace that proves you thought about it

```trace
{
  "input": "player sends \"gg\" just as the connection drops",
  "lanes": [
    { "id": "st", "label": "message state", "kind": "phases", "of": ["pending", "sent", "failed", "retry", "acked"] },
    { "id": "ui", "label": "what the player sees", "kind": "log" }
  ],
  "vars": ["id", "outbox", "server copies"],
  "steps": [
    {
      "note": "The client mints an id and appends locally. The message is on screen before a byte leaves the machine.",
      "cursors": { "st": { "at": "pending" } },
      "marks": { "st": { "pending": "active" } },
      "cells": { "ui": ["gg  ·  sending…"] },
      "vars": { "id": "a1f", "outbox": "[a1f]", "server copies": "0" }
    },
    {
      "note": "The frame goes out and the server **does** store it as seq 42 — but the connection dies before the ack comes back.",
      "cursors": { "st": { "at": "sent" } },
      "marks": { "st": { "pending": "done", "sent": "active" } },
      "cells": { "ui": ["gg  ·  sending…"] },
      "vars": { "id": "a1f", "outbox": "[a1f]", "server copies": "1 (seq 42)" }
    },
    {
      "note": "No ack inside the timeout. The message is marked **failed** — visibly, with a retry affordance. It is still in the outbox.",
      "cursors": { "st": { "at": "failed" } },
      "marks": { "st": { "sent": "done", "failed": "bad" } },
      "cells": { "ui": ["gg  ·  ⚠ not sent — tap to retry"] },
      "vars": { "id": "a1f", "outbox": "[a1f]", "server copies": "1 (seq 42)" }
    },
    {
      "note": "Reconnect flushes the outbox. The retry carries **the same id `a1f`** — this is the only reason the next step is not a duplicate.",
      "cursors": { "st": { "at": "retry" } },
      "marks": { "st": { "failed": "done", "retry": "window" } },
      "cells": { "ui": ["gg  ·  sending…"] },
      "vars": { "id": "a1f", "outbox": "[a1f]", "server copies": "1 (seq 42)" }
    },
    {
      "note": "The server recognises `a1f`, does not store a second copy, and replies with the original seq. The client reconciles and the outbox drains.",
      "cursors": { "st": { "at": "acked" } },
      "marks": { "st": { "retry": "done", "acked": "hit" } },
      "cells": { "ui": ["gg  ·  ✓ 14:02"] },
      "vars": { "id": "a1f", "outbox": "[]", "server copies": "1 (seq 42)" }
    }
  ],
  "result": "one message in the channel — the id made the retry safe, the seq made it sortable"
}
```

Without the client-side id, step 5 posts "gg" twice and the player looks like they are spamming.

## Reconnect and backfill

```javascript
ws.onopen = () => {
  // Never "give me new messages". Always "give me what I missed."
  send({ type: "subscribe", channels, since: store.lastSeqByChannel() });
  flushOutbox();
};
```

- **Resume from `lastSeq`, per channel.** Resuming from "now" loses everything sent during the outage, silently — no error, no gap, just messages the player never sees.
- **Detect gaps on the live path too.** If you hold up to seq 104 and 107 arrives, request 105–106 rather than rendering out of order.
- **Cap the backfill.** After a long disconnect, do not replay four hours of global chat. Return the last N plus a "you missed 2,400 messages" marker.
- **Backoff with jitter** on the reconnect itself, or a server restart brings every client back at the same instant and knocks it over again.

## Presence and typing — deliberately lossy

The opposite design from messages, and saying so is a good signal:

- **Typing** is throttled (one event per ~2s while typing, not per keystroke), expires on a client-side timer, and is never retried. A stale "typing…" is worse than a missing one.
- **Presence** is a heartbeat plus a server-side TTL, not an `online`/`offline` event pair — because the `offline` event is exactly the one a crashed client fails to send. Debounce the UI so a two-second blip does not flicker the roster.
- Neither goes in the outbox. They are worthless late.

## Moderation and abuse

An interviewer at any company that has shipped a game will ask. The rule is one line:

**Client-side is UX, server-side is truth.**

- **Mute/block** — filter locally for instant feedback, *and* on the server so the payload never arrives.
- **Rate limit** — disable the input locally after N messages in a window for a good experience; enforce on the server because the client is under the attacker's control.
- **Profanity filter** — server-side, because a client-side word list ships the word list.
- **Report** — needs the message `id` and `seq`, which you have, plus server-retained context.

## Rendering the log

The part people forget is a UI question, and it is the one Acceldata-shaped interviewers push into:

- **Virtualize** — a session can be thousands of messages; see [virtualized lists](/system-design/306). Variable heights, because messages wrap.
- **Stick to bottom, but only if you were at the bottom.** If the player scrolled up to read, new messages must not yank the viewport. Show a "3 new messages ↓" pill instead.
- **Anchor the scroll on prepend.** Loading older history above the viewport must not move what is on screen — measure, prepend, restore `scrollTop` by the delta.
- **Batch renders.** At 50 messages/sec in a busy global channel, coalesce arrivals into one `requestAnimationFrame` (the pattern in [real-time transports](/system-design/105)), or the main thread is the bottleneck and the transport is fine.
- **Unread divider** that survives a re-render, and a jump-to-latest.

## Edge cases to raise unprompted

- Two messages in flight; the ack for the second arrives first.
- The same account open in two tabs — a `SharedWorker` or leader election, not two sockets.
- Auth token expires mid-connection: re-auth in-band, or reconnect and resume.
- A message that fails permanently — it must stay visible and retryable, not vanish.
- Very long message, emoji, RTL, and a paste of 10,000 characters.
- Channel membership changes while you have unread in it (kicked from the team).
- Clock skew — the reason `serverTs` is what you render, not `sentAt`.

## Common mistakes

- **Server-generated ids.** Now a retry is a duplicate and you cannot safely retry anything.
- **Reconciling the ack by position.** Breaks the instant two sends overlap.
- **Sorting by client timestamp.** Clocks are wrong; in a game, sometimes deliberately.
- **Resuming from "now".** The outage window is lost in silence.
- **Retrying typing indicators.** They are worthless late — drop them.
- **Auto-scrolling unconditionally.** Yanks the viewport out from under someone reading.
- **One render per message.** The transport is fine; the main thread is on fire.

## Key takeaways

- Client makes the id, server makes the order. That split is the answer to most follow-ups.
- Optimistic append plus an outbox is what makes it feel instant *and* survive a disconnect.
- Reconcile by id; resume from a per-channel seq; detect gaps rather than hoping.
- Chat is reliable-and-ordered; presence and typing are lossy on purpose. Different problems, different guarantees.
- Client-side moderation is user experience; server-side is the actual control.
- The log is a [virtualized list](/react-guide/16) with a stick-to-bottom rule and batched renders — the UI half is graded too.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"Two players send at the same instant — who is first?"** — Whoever the server sequences first. Both clients re-sort on ack; neither client's clock is consulted.
- **"The ack never comes. What does the player see?"** — The message stays on screen marked as failed with a retry, never disappears, and retries with the same id so it cannot duplicate.
- **"10,000 players in global chat?"** — Fan-out is the server's problem, but the client's is now rate: sample or collapse, batch renders per frame, and cap the retained buffer.
- **"How is this different from position sync?"** — Chat wants reliable and ordered; positions want the newest and tolerate loss. Put positions on datagrams, or at minimum a separate channel that drops rather than queues.
- **"Two tabs open?"** — One socket in a `SharedWorker`, tabs as views onto it. Otherwise you double the connections and deliver every message twice.
